title: Georgia Bureaucratic Deference Elimination Act; enact
synopsis: The Georgia Bureaucratic Deference Elimination Act amends Chapter 1 of Title 15 to bar courts and administrative officers from deferring to an agency's interpretation of a statute or regulation. Previously, Georgia courts and hearing officers could give weight to an agency's construction of the laws it administers and of its own rules; that interpretive question is now for the tribunal to decide without such deference. The change reaches any proceeding in which an agency's reading of a statute or rule is at issue, including administrative hearings and judicial review of agency action.
impact: Agency readings of statutes and rules no longer carry deference, opening regulatory interpretations to de novo challenge in administrative and civil proceedings.

title: Motor vehicles; proper operation upon approach by an authorized emergency vehicle or by a law enforcement vehicle for purposes of a traffic stop; provide
synopsis: The Act amends Title 40 to prescribe how a motorist must operate a vehicle when approached by an authorized emergency vehicle, and separately when approached by a law enforcement vehicle attempting to initiate a traffic stop. Georgia's existing rules of the road addressed yielding to emergency vehicles displaying audible and visual signals; the Act now also sets out the driver's obligations in the traffic-stop context. Because these are statutory rules of the road, violations supply a negligence per se theory in motor vehicle cases and a comparative-fault argument against a plaintiff driver.
impact: Creates new Title 40 driver duties usable as negligence per se or comparative fault in auto cases involving emergency vehicles and traffic stops.

title: Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions
synopsis: HB295 amends Chapter 60 of Title 36 (general provisions for counties and municipalities) to create a statutory procedure by which real property owners may present claims to a local government for lost property value or expenses caused by that government's failure to comply with or enforce specified laws, ordinances, and resolutions, or by the local government's maintenance of a public nuisance. Previously, such claims against counties and cities proceeded under general tort, nuisance, and inverse condemnation theories subject to sovereign and official immunity defenses and generally applicable ante litem notice rules, with no dedicated compensation-claim mechanism in Chapter 60. The provided title and description do not specify the claim filing deadlines, notice content, response obligations, damages measures or caps, or whether and when suit may follow an unpaid claim, so those details must be confirmed from the enrolled text.
impact: Creates a new administrative claim path against Georgia local governments for property-value losses from nonenforcement or public nuisance, adding a pre-suit step to counsel.

title: Middle Judicial Circuit; superior courts; provide for a third judge
synopsis: This act amends O.C.G.A. § 15-6-2, which sets the number of superior court judges by circuit, to add a third superior court judgeship in the Middle Judicial Circuit. The initial occupant of the new seat is appointed by the Governor, with the term provided for in the act. The governing authorities of the counties comprising the circuit are authorized to furnish facilities, office space, supplies, equipment, and personnel for the judges, and the act declares the court's inherent authority.
impact: Adds a third superior court bench in the Middle Judicial Circuit, changing judge assignment and calendaring for civil cases filed there.

title: Trey's Law; enact
synopsis: Enacted as "Trey's Law," this act amends Article 8 of Chapter 11 of Title 9 (provisional and final remedies and special proceedings) to declare contrary to Georgia public policy any contract or agreement having the purpose or effect of concealing the details of a claim of childhood sexual abuse. Previously, confidentiality and nondisclosure terms in settlements of such claims were generally enforceable as ordinary contract provisions; going forward, such concealment provisions run against declared public policy. The act separately provides for confidentiality of identifying information of childhood sexual abuse victims.
impact: Defense counsel and insurers can no longer rely on nondisclosure terms to keep childhood sexual abuse claim details confidential, though victim identifying information remains protected.

title: Courts; certain shareholder claims to be brought before the Georgia State-wide Business Court; provide
synopsis: Amends Titles 14 and 15 to route certain shareholder claims to the Georgia State-wide Business Court. A corporation may now use its articles of incorporation or bylaws to require that covered claims be heard there, and the Act provides a removal mechanism for moving such claims to the Business Court; previously, placement in the Business Court generally depended on the parties' election rather than a charter or bylaw forum provision. The Act also addresses attorney's fees and costs in connection with these claims, with exemptions from payment in specified situations, and supplies governing definitions.
impact: Shareholder and corporate-governance disputes may now be channeled by charter or bylaw into the Business Court, with removal available and fee exposure attached.

title: Increasing Access to Contraceptives Act; enact
synopsis: The Increasing Access to Contraceptives Act amends the pharmacy practice article (O.C.G.A. Title 26, Ch. 4, Art. 3) to authorize pharmacists, in specified circumstances, to dispense self-administered hormonal contraceptives and to administer injectable hormonal contraceptives — conduct that previously required dispensing on another prescriber's order. It amends the general insurance provisions of O.C.G.A. Title 33, Ch. 24, Art. 1 to set minimum quantities of certain contraceptives that insurers must provide, and makes conforming changes to the Medicaid article at O.C.G.A. Title 49, Ch. 4, Art. 7. It also amends the Georgia Composite Medical Board article (O.C.G.A. Title 43, Ch. 34, Art. 1) to waive civil liability, criminal culpability, and professional discipline in defined circumstances.
impact: Creates a new insurer contraceptive-supply mandate and a defined civil immunity that may be asserted in pharmacist and prescriber liability claims.

title: Preston Fant and Brant Chesney Firefighter Safety Act; enact
synopsis: The Preston Fant and Brant Chesney Firefighter Safety Act amends Chapter 2 of Title 25 (regulation of fire and other hazards) to require that notice be posted on certain buildings identifying the use of light-frame truss-type construction. The Act provides definitions, authorizes rules and regulations to implement the posting requirement, and provides for enforcement. Building owners and operators within the covered class now carry an affirmative marking obligation they did not have under prior Chapter 2 provisions.
impact: Creates a statutory posting duty that plaintiffs may invoke as a negligence per se or notice theory in premises and fire-loss litigation.

title: Motor vehicles; personal delivery devices; revise operation procedures and restrictions
synopsis: The Act amends Part 2A of Article 13 of Chapter 6 of Title 40, the portion of the motor vehicle code governing electric personal assistive mobility devices and personal delivery devices, to revise the operation procedures and restrictions that apply to personal delivery devices. Previously, PDD operation on sidewalks, crosswalks, and roadways was governed by the operating requirements as previously enacted in that Part; those requirements are now revised, though the provided description does not state which specific procedures changed. Practitioners handling claims involving sidewalk delivery robots should pull the current text of Part 2A rather than relying on prior versions.
impact: Revised statutory operating rules for delivery robots reset the negligence per se and comparative-fault baseline in pedestrian and vehicle collision claims involving personal delivery devices.

title: Banking and finance; holds on accounts of eligible adults for suspected financial exploitation; provide
synopsis: The Act amends Title 7 (banking and finance) to authorize financial institutions to place temporary holds on accounts of eligible adults when financial exploitation is suspected, and sets procedures for placing and lifting those holds. On the litigation finance side, it adds cease and desist procedures aimed at persons providing litigation finance without registration, creates a path for judicial hearings to review Department decisions on litigation finance matters, and imposes disclosure obligations on registrants. It also drops the requirement that independent credit reports be obtained from a consumer reporting agency as defined in the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, adds definitions, and makes conforming changes.
impact: Counsel handling funded claims should track new disclosure duties, unregistered-funder cease and desist exposure, and the judicial review route for Department litigation finance decisions.

title: Professions and businesses; repeal and reenact Chapter 11A, the Dietetics Practice Act
synopsis: HB185 repeals and reenacts OCGA Title 43, Chapter 11A, the Dietetics Practice Act, and makes conforming cross-reference amendments in Titles 9 (civil practice), 31, 33 (insurance), 43, and 51 (torts). The description identifies the Title 9, 33, and 51 changes only as conforming cross-references, so the substantive civil-practice rules appear unchanged; the provided text does not identify which specific code sections (for example, the professional malpractice affidavit or expert competency provisions that enumerate licensed dietitians) are being renumbered or relabeled. Practitioners relying on statutory references to dietitians or the prior chapter should verify current section numbers and any changed licensure terminology in the reenacted chapter.
impact: Renumbered dietetics licensure references may alter citations in malpractice affidavit, expert competency, and insurance statutes without changing substantive civil rules.

title: State Board of Workers' Compensation; notice of eligibility for compensation to an injured employee to his or her legal guardian; provide
synopsis: Amends O.C.G.A. § 34-9-26 and § 35-1-24 so that the required notice of eligibility for compensation for an injured employee is provided to the employee's legal guardian — by the State Board of Workers' Compensation under Title 34 and by law enforcement agencies under § 35-1-24. Previously those notice duties ran to the injured officer/employee. It also amends the Georgia State Indemnification Fund provisions (Title 45, Ch. 9, Art. 5, Pt. 1) to create an application window for eligible individuals incapacitated by organic brain damage sustained in the line of duty on or before July 1, 2024, subject to automatic repeal.
impact: Counsel handling incapacitated first-responder claims should confirm guardian notice was given and calendar the limited indemnification-fund application window for pre-July 2024 brain injuries.

title: Motor vehicles; federal regulations regarding safe operation of commercial motor carriers and commercial vehicles; update reference date
synopsis: O.C.G.A. § 40-1-8 incorporates the federal motor carrier safety regulations and hazardous materials rules into Georgia law by reference as of a fixed date, and adopting them for intrastate carriers. This Act moves that reference date forward, so the federal rules as amended through the newer date now control, and it revises a definition used in the Code section. The provided description does not identify the new reference date or the definition revised.
impact: Trucking cases must be measured against the newly incorporated version of the federal safety regulations, which govern negligence per se and standard-of-care theories.

title: Civil practice; require depositions to be taken before certified court reporters
synopsis: Amends Article 5 of Chapter 11 of Title 9 (depositions and discovery) to require that depositions taken in Georgia be taken before a certified court reporter. It also repeals the existing requirement that depositions taken in this state be recorded by stenographic means. The result shifts the statutory focus from the method of recording to the qualification of the officer before whom the deposition is taken.
impact: Georgia depositions must now be taken before a certified court reporter, replacing the prior requirement that they be stenographically recorded.

title: Motor vehicles; exempt ride share drivers or ride share network services from definition of motor carrier
synopsis: HB339 amends Georgia's motor carrier article (Title 40, Chapter 1, Article 3) to expressly exclude ride share drivers and ride share network services from the definition of "motor carrier," adds definitions, and revises the article's legislative findings. It also provides that ride share network services are not liable for the actions of ride share drivers in certain circumstances, and makes conforming changes elsewhere in the article. Because the motor carrier designation is the gateway to the regulatory and insurance-related obligations imposed by that article, drivers and network services operating under this exemption are no longer treated as motor carriers for those purposes. The bill text as described does not spell out which circumstances trigger the liability exemption or how it interacts with any other basis for holding a network service liable, so those limits must be read from the enacted language itself.
impact: Ride share drivers and networks fall outside motor carrier status, narrowing claims and insurer-joinder theories that depend on that designation.

title: Greene County Public Facilities Authority Act; enact
synopsis: This local act creates the Greene County Public Facilities Authority, an entity that did not previously exist, and sets out its membership, powers, purposes, and authority to issue revenue bonds. Of direct relevance to litigators, the act includes provisions on tort immunity for the authority and fixes the venue and jurisdiction of actions involving it, along with provisions on moneys received and trust funds and tax exemption. Counsel handling claims arising from facilities or projects in Greene County should confirm whether the authority is the correct defendant and how its immunity and venue provisions apply before filing.
impact: Adds a Greene County public authority defendant with statutory tort immunity and fixed venue and jurisdiction for actions against it.

title: Fulton County; State Court; provide additional judge
synopsis: This local Act amends the 1976 consolidation Act creating the State Court of Fulton County (as amended in 1994 and 2003) to add two judgeships to that court, increasing its bench to twelve judges. The two additional judges are to be appointed by the Governor as soon as practicable after the Act's effective date, for terms beginning on the date of appointment and expiring December 31, 2026, and until successors are elected and qualified; thereafter the seats are filled by election. The additional judges have the same powers and privileges as the other judges of the court, and provision is made for compensation and expenses.
impact: Fulton County State Court gains two judges, bringing its bench to twelve and adding civil trial capacity in a high-volume venue for tort and insurance-defense cases.

title: Motor vehicles; federal regulations regarding safe operation of commercial motor vehicle and carriers; update reference date
synopsis: HB114 amends O.C.G.A. § 40-1-8 to update the reference date for incorporating federal safety regulations governing motor carriers, commercial motor vehicles, drivers, and hazardous-materials transport, and revises a definition within that section. The effect is to align Georgia's adopted federal safety standards with a more current version of the federal regulations. The bill text does not specify the new reference date or which definition is revised.
impact: Updated federal safety standards now apply as the negligence-per-se benchmark in commercial motor vehicle and trucking cases.

title: Insurance; medically necessary expenses for standard fertility preservation services when a medically necessary treatment for cancer, sickle cell disease, or lupus may directly or indirectly cause an impairment of fertility; require coverage
synopsis: Amends Chapter 24 of Title 33 to require certain insurance policies to cover medically necessary expenses for standard fertility preservation services when a medically necessary treatment for cancer, sickle cell disease, or lupus may directly or indirectly impair fertility. The Act provides definitions, exclusions, permissible cost-sharing, and authorizes implementing rules and regulations. The prior rule did not mandate this specific coverage; the text does not spell out the full scope of affected policies here.
impact: Expands mandated insurance coverage, potentially generating coverage disputes over fertility-preservation benefits tied to cancer, sickle cell, or lupus treatment.

title: Appellate practice; digital recording of certain trial proceedings; provide
synopsis: HB 179 amends the appellate practice provisions of O.C.G.A. Title 5, Chapter 6, Article 2, along with Title 9, Article 2 of Chapter 14 (post-conviction procedure) and Title 15 (courts, including the Georgia State-wide Business Court), to authorize digital recording of specified trial proceedings and to set rules governing the use and regulation of digital recording systems, with accompanying definitions. Previously, the statutory framework for making the record in these proceedings did not expressly provide for digital recording as an authorized method; the Act now supplies that authorization and its parameters. The description does not identify which specific proceedings may be digitally recorded, what certification or transcription requirements apply, or how a digital recording is to be reduced to a transcript for the record on appeal, so those details must be read in the enacted text.
impact: Civil litigators may face digitally recorded proceedings, including in the Business Court, changing how the record and appellate transcript are created and verified.

title: Education; safety, health, and well-being of students and school communities; provide
synopsis: HB 268 amends Chapter 2 of Title 20 to create an Office of Safe Schools within GEMA/HS, to require technical assistance for local school systems in developing threat management team policies and procedures, and to establish a state-wide behavioral threat management operational process with accompanying definitions. It also amends O.C.G.A. 16-11-37 to criminalize threatening death or serious injury to persons who are or are likely to be at school, and amends Article 4 of Chapter 18 of Title 50 to exempt certain records from public inspection. The text supplied does not identify which specific records fall within the Open Records exemption, nor does it state any immunity provisions for schools or threat management team members.
impact: Creates statutory school threat-assessment duties relevant to negligent security claims while shielding some related records from Open Records requests.
